content: Before the introduction of pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs), Streptococcus pneumoniae was the most frequently isolated pathogen from the middle ear fluid of children with acute otitis media (AOM). By reducing nasopharyngeal colonization of this bacterium, PCVs have the potential to decrease the incidence of AOM. However, post-PCV studies have reported a shift in causative pathogens toward non-vaccine serotypes and other bacteria, necessitating ongoing evaluation of the vaccines' effects. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy of PCVs in preventing AOM in children up to 12 years of age. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing PCVs to placebo or control vaccines. The primary outcomes were the frequency of all-cause AOM and adverse effects, while secondary outcomes included the frequency of pneumococcal AOM and recurrent AOM (defined as three or more episodes in six months or four or more in one year). The certainty of the evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. Fifteen publications from 11 trials, involving a total of 60,733 children, were included in the review. These trials evaluated 7to 11-valent PCVs compared to control vaccines, such as meningococcus type C vaccine or hepatitis A/B vaccines. Most studies were funded by pharmaceutical companies, and the overall risk of bias was low. Seven trials (59,415 children) administered PCVs during early infancy, while four trials (1,318 children) included older children aged one year and above, some of whom had a history of respiratory illness. Due to significant clinical heterogeneity, results were reported for individual studies. PCV Administration in Early Infancy 1. CRM197-PCV7 (7-valent PCV with CRM197 as the carrier protein): In low-risk infants, CRM197-PCV7 was associated with a 6% relative risk reduction (RRR) in all-cause AOM (95% confidence interval [CI]: −4% to 16%; moderate-certainty evidence). However, no reduction was observed in high-risk infants (RRR −5%; 95% CI: −25% to 12%). For pneumococcal AOM, CRM197-PCV7 showed a 20% RRR (95% CI: 7% to 31%; high-certainty evidence). For recurrent AOM, CRM197-PCV7 demonstrated a 9% RRR (95% CI: −12% to 27%; moderate-certainty evidence). 2. OMPC-PCV7 (7-valent PCV with outer membrane protein complex of Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B as the carrier protein): OMPC-PCV7 did not reduce all-cause AOM (RRR −1%; 95% CI: −12% to 10%; low-certainty evidence). However, it was associated with a 25% RRR in pneumococcal AOM (95% CI: 11% to 37%; high-certainty evidence). 3. PHiD-CV10/11 (10and 11-valent PCVs conjugated to protein D of Haemophilus influenzae): PHiD-CV10 showed a variable effect on all-cause AOM, with RRRs ranging from 6% (95% CI: −6% to 17%) to 15% (95% CI: −1% to 28%; low-certainty evidence). PHiD-CV11 was associated with a 34% RRR in all-cause AOM (95% CI: 21% to 44%; moderate-certainty evidence). Both PHiD-CV10 and PHiD-CV11 demonstrated significant reductions in pneumococcal AOM, with RRRs of 53% (95% CI: 16% to 74%) and 52% (95% CI: 37% to 63%), respectively (high-certainty evidence). PHiD-CV11 also showed a 56% RRR in recurrent AOM (95% CI: −2% to 80%; low-certainty evidence). PCV Administration at a Later Age 1. CRM197-PCV7: In children aged 1 to 7 years with a history of respiratory illness or frequent AOM, CRM197-PCV7 did not reduce all-cause AOM (moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, no benefit was observed when CRM197-PCV7 was combined with a trivalent influenza vaccine in children aged 18 to 72 months with a history of respiratory tract infections. 2. CRM197-PCV9 (9-valent PCV): In one trial involving healthy daycare attendees aged 1 to 3 years, CRM197-PCV9 was associated with a 17% RRR in parent-reported all-cause otitis media (95% CI: −2% to 33%; very low-certainty evidence). Adverse Events Nine trials reported on adverse effects, involving 77,389 children. Mild local reactions (redness, swelling) and fever were more common in the PCV groups compared to control vaccine groups: Redness (<2.5 cm): 5% to 20% in PCV groups versus 0% to 16% in control groups. Swelling (<2.5 cm): 5% to 12% in PCV groups versus 0% to 8% in control groups. Fever (<39°C): 15% to 44% in PCV groups versus 8% to 25% in control groups. More severe reactions, such as redness or swelling >2.5 cm and fever >39°C, were rare and did not differ significantly between PCV and control groups. Pain or tenderness was more frequently reported in PCV groups (3% to 38%) compared to control groups (0% to 8%). Serious adverse events causally related to vaccination were rare, and no fatal events were reported. Authors' Conclusions The administration of CRM197-PCV7 and PHiD-CV10 during early infancy is associated with significant reductions in pneumococcal AOM. However, the evidence for their effects on all-cause AOM is less certain, with lowto moderate-certainty evidence. No benefit was observed for PCV administration in high-risk infants, older children, or after early infancy. PCVs were associated with an increase in mild local reactions, fever, and pain, but there was no significant difference in severe adverse events compared to control vaccines.
